messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 54
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Business Owner
- Trauma Type: Relief worker in war zone
- Pcl5: 69

He is a 54-year-old Latin American man who built a modest but successful business over many years, and for much of his adult life he has seen himself as steady, practical, and capable of carrying other people’s burdens. He is married, deeply attached to his wife, and proud of the life they have created together. Before the war work, he describes himself as someone who handled stress well. He had dealt with long hours, financial pressure, and the normal demands of owning a business, but he still felt anchored by routine, family dinners, and the sense that his days followed a familiar shape.

That changed when he took relief work in a war zone, initially telling himself that he was going for a short time and that his experience organizing resources would be useful. He remembers arriving with a sense of purpose. The work demanded constant movement: unloading supplies, coordinating local staff, trying to keep track of lists of injured people, food, fuel, and medicines. The setting quickly became defined by sirens, smoke, the sound of distant explosions, and the faces of families waiting in line with the strained, watchful look of people who do not know if they will be safe by nightfall. He says he tried not to think too much and focused instead on what needed to be done next.

Over time, the violence around him became more personal. He witnessed bodies in the street, saw wounded children brought in with improvised bandages, and heard people speaking in tones that he understood only partially but could still read in their fear. One day, after a nearby strike, he helped carry survivors from a collapsed building. He remembers dust in his mouth, the smell of concrete and blood, and the feeling that the world had suddenly become unreal. A few moments stand out with particular force: a mother screaming for her missing son, a man staring blankly while clutching a child’s shoe, the sudden silence after a blast when everyone seems to wait for the next one. He does not describe one single event as the worst; rather, he describes being worn down by the accumulation of horror and the constant sense that catastrophe could happen at any second.

When he returns home, his wife notices first that he is different in ways that are hard to name at first. He is physically present but seems to drift away in the middle of conversations. He sits at the dinner table and suddenly stops talking, as if he has gone elsewhere. Small noises make him tense. A car backfiring, a door slamming, even a mop bucket dropping in the street can send his whole body into alert. He begins checking locks repeatedly and insisting on knowing where everyone is in the house. He keeps the television low but cannot tolerate silence either. At night, he sleeps in fragments. He falls asleep exhausted and wakes abruptly with his heart racing, often after dreams that leave him sweaty and disoriented. He does not always remember the details, only the feeling that he is again among rubble, trying to find someone before it is too late.

He finds himself avoiding anything that reminds him of the war zone. News footage, certain smells, even Spanish-language reports about conflict can pull him into a state of agitation and nausea. He no longer wants to hear stories of suffering from clients or friends, although he feels guilty about that distance. As a business owner, he still shows up and keeps things moving, but he notices that his concentration is not what it used to be. He rereads invoices, loses his train of thought in meetings, and becomes unusually irritable when employees ask him the same question twice. He is embarrassed by how quickly he snaps, then spends hours afterward replaying the exchange and wondering why he cannot just be the man he used to be.

At home, he is loving but less available. His wife says he looks permanently tired. He wants comfort and also feels uncomfortable being touched unexpectedly. Intimacy has become complicated by his sense that he must stay on guard. He misses the version of himself that returned from work and could relax into ordinary life, but he also feels an unspoken obligation not to burden others with what he saw. Much of his distress remains held inside, where it comes out as tension in his jaw, a clenched posture, and a persistent sense that something terrible is still about to happen. Even in calm moments, he does not feel fully safe. He lives as if part of him remains in the war zone, listening for the next impact, trying to stay ready.
